dashboard.verdict.released.detail: Every package built, every signature verified, and the whole set replaced the repository your system updates from.
dashboard.verdict.testFailed: Held in testing — the installation test failed.
dashboard.verdict.testFailed.detail: Every package built and was signed, but an unattended installation of the set did not succeed, so it was not released. Your system still installs the previous release.
dashboard.verdict.inTesting.detail: Every package built and was signed, and the set is in the testing repository awaiting a check. Your system still installs the previous release.
dashboard.verdict.built.detail: The build host holds no signing key. Signing and publishing happen afterwards on a separate machine.
dashboard.verdict.heldBack.detail: One package did not pass, so the whole set stayed where it was. A partial update is never shipped.
dashboard.verdict.incomplete.detail: The record was written before the run reached a verdict.
dashboard.test.passed: This repository was installed unattended into a virtual machine, and the installed system booted and answered for itself.
dashboard.test.installed: This repository installed, but the installed system never came up, so it was not released.
dashboard.test.installing: An unattended installation of this repository never finished, so it was not released.
dashboard.test.failed: An unattended installation of this repository did not succeed, which is why it was not released.
landing.hero.title: An installer that knows what it’s doing.
landing.hero.lede: Vanilla Arch underneath. A configuration knowledge base on top — every setting, every interaction between settings, transparently encoded.
landing.principles.title: Three principles, applied throughout.
landing.principles.transparent.title: Every choice is data
landing.principles.transparent.body: Settings, dependencies, and lifecycle scripts live in a KDL knowledge base — auditable, forkable, fetched at install time so improvements ship without re-spinning an ISO.
landing.principles.hardened.title: Security by default
landing.principles.hardened.body: Per-CPU vulnerability mitigation, system hardening sysctls, restricted user namespaces, optional hardened_malloc. Opt-out, not opt-in — and every trade-off is explained where you make it.
landing.principles.desktops.title: XFCE · Wayfire · Niri · COSMIC
landing.principles.desktops.body: Pick one, or install all four side by side and switch from the greeter. Wayfire and Niri come with waybar, nwg-launchers and nwgbar already configured; XFCE and COSMIC bring their own panels. None of them is a stripped-down minimum.
landing.desktops.title: Four equal desktops, not one default and three afterthoughts.
landing.desktops.lede: Wayfire and Niri are commonly considered incomplete environments. Ditana ships everything they need — a polished waybar, nwg-launcher, nwgbar, and a consistent panel layout — and treats all four desktops as first-class citizens.
landing.desktops.xfce.alt: XFCE on Ditana with Blue Flat theme, Firefox, Thunar
landing.desktops.xfce.caption: XFCE — Xorg, mature, fast
landing.desktops.wayfire.alt: Wayfire on Ditana with Blue Vibrant theme, Brave, Thunar
landing.desktops.wayfire.caption: Wayfire — Wayland, Compiz-inspired
landing.desktops.niri.alt: Niri on Ditana with Blue Vibrant theme, Brave, COSMIC Files
landing.desktops.niri.caption: Niri — Wayland, scrollable tiling
landing.desktops.cosmic.alt: COSMIC on Ditana with Amber Rounded theme, LibreWolf, Thunar
landing.desktops.cosmic.caption: COSMIC — Wayland, System76’s Rust desktop
landing.snapshots.title: Every upgrade is reversible.
landing.snapshots.lede: Arch’s rolling-release model is a feature, not a bug — but it can land breakage on a Tuesday morning. Ditana takes the sting out by snapshotting the system before every upgrade, automatically.
landing.snapshots.subtitle: Atomic snapshots, taken by a pacman hook.
landing.snapshots.alt: System maintenance dialog showing automatic system snapshots option enabled by default
landing.snapshots.p1: On ZFS and BTRFS, snapshots are atomic and free — a few milliseconds before any package upgrade. On XFS and EXT4, Timeshift handles the same job via rsync, completing typical incremental snapshots in seconds.
landing.snapshots.p2: The first snapshot is created by the installer itself, just before the first reboot. That means you can roll back to a freshly-installed system from day one — no setup, no first-upgrade chicken-and-egg.
landing.snapshots.p3: System snapshots, not data snapshots: /home and other data volumes are never touched. Roll back the system; keep your work.
landing.snapshots.p4: For ZFS, Ditana ships its own zfs-autosnap fork that — unlike the upstream — removes the pacman lock file from the snapshot, so a rollback leaves you with a working pacman immediately.
landing.headless.title: Headless too.
landing.headless.body: System hardening plus automatic snapshots make Ditana a viable Arch-based server choice — uncommon for a rolling release. The installer’s Server profile skips the desktop install entirely and leans into the security defaults.
landing.hardware.title: It checks the upstream sources at install time.
landing.hardware.nvidia.alt: NVIDIA driver decision dialog with detected PCI ID and recommendation rationale
landing.hardware.nvidia.title: NVIDIA detection, four-way decision.
landing.hardware.nvidia.p1: Ditana queries the live PCI ID lists from github.com/NVIDIA/open-gpu-kernel-modules and the official legacy GPU page at install time. Based on the result, it recommends one of four driver options – nvidia-open-dkms, the legacy proprietary nvidia-580xx-dkms, the older nvidia-470xx-dkms, or nouveau – and checks that the package it is about to recommend is present in the repository, reverting to nouveau when it is not.
landing.hardware.nvidia.p2: It then explains what it picked, and why.
landing.cpu.title: CPU vulnerabilities, detected and mitigated.
landing.cpu.p1: Spectre v2, Meltdown, MDS, TAA, MMIO Stale Data, RETBleed, SRSO, GDS, RFDS — Ditana reads /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/ at install time, enables only the mitigations your CPU actually needs, and lets you review each one with documentation.
landing.cpu.p2: Every mitigation comes with its cost spelled out, so you can make an informed call instead of choosing between “secure default” and “fast default” blindly.
landing.cpu.alt: CPU vulnerability mitigation dialog showing detected vulnerabilities and selectable mitigations
landing.hardening.title: System hardening, opt-out by default.
landing.hardening.body: Unprivileged user namespaces restricted to the programs that need them. Restricted ptrace. Hidden kernel pointers. Hardened FIFO and regular-file protection in sticky directories. SYN cookies, no ICMP redirects, no source routing, reverse-path filtering. Each option ships enabled, each one is explained – and developers get a profile that loosens the right things for debugging.
landing.installer.title: Ten categories. Sensible defaults. No mystery.
landing.installer.lede: Tell the installer who you are – originating from a different distribution, migrating from KDE Plasma, Cinnamon, Xfce or MATE, working as a developer, running as a server, or falling into none of these – and it accordingly pre-flips checkboxes. You may examine and revise every single one prior to the start of installation.
landing.installer.categories.title: One screen, the whole system.
landing.installer.categories.body: Configuration categories let you drill into desktops, browsers, file managers, office suites, AI tools, terminals, kernels, filesystems, hardening, mitigations, and the system allocator — all from one menu, all reversible, all explained.
landing.installer.impact.title: Every change comes with its impact.
landing.installer.impact.body: Toggle an option, see the consequence: which packages get added, which scripts will run, what other settings flip in response. The settings graph is data — Ditana shows you the path through it.
landing.installer.impact.alt: Settings impact overview showing dependent changes
landing.config.title: The installer is small. The knowledge base is big.
landing.config.lede: A Linux installer should do more than partition, install packages, and hand off. PKGBUILDs only know about their own package — they can’t know what else is on the system. Ditana keeps the cross-cutting decisions in a separate, auditable knowledge base.
landing.config.kdl.title: Settings declare their dependencies in plain KDL.
landing.config.kdl.body: This excerpt says: install kitty only if the chosen terminal operates on Wayland alone and XFCE is also installed. Nobody would consider requesting that, and nobody needs to: the rule stands beside the package list, where a reviewer can see both the condition and the reason for it, rather than being hidden within installer code.
landing.final.title: Ready to try it?
landing.final.body: Ditana {{release}} is a {{size}} ISO with a detached GPG signature. It fetches its packages and its configuration while it installs, so a working network connection is part of the requirements. The full install takes 15–45 minutes depending on what you pick.
